Following bench validation, the reformer was installed at SwRI’s MRF, which provides a closed-loop natural-gas flow system capable of delivering up to 500 SLPM at pressures to 60 psig. Testing at the MRF covered flow rates from 50 to 500 SLPM and pressures between 10 and 30 psig to define the upper limit of plasma stability and to evaluate pressure-dependent discharge behavior under realistic gas velocities. Data from the MRF campaign were used to confirm the operational envelope and to inform design refinements prior to engine testing. The final test phase involved integration of the reformer with natural-gas engines to evaluate performance under relevant scale operating conditions. The reformer was first coupled to the fuel line of a Cooper AJAX 2802 ULE engine rated at 384 brake horsepower (bhp) and 440 revolutions per minute (rpm) and subsequently installed on a Cummins X15N engine rated at 400 bhp and 1,900 rpm. Exhaust measurements were obtained using Fourier-Transform Infrared (FTIR) Spectroscopy to quantify CH , CO , NO , and volatile organic compound (VOC) concentrations, while in-cylinder pressure 4 2 x transducers provided combustion metrics for evaluating variability, stability, and efficiency improvements resulting from the plasma-reformed fuel. 2.3.5 Data Analysis and Verification Statistical filtering was applied to all exhaust and plasma-diagnostic data to remove random noise with variations below 0.5 percent. Methane conversion efficiency was determined by measuring the difference in methane leaks between plasma reformer operation and bypass mode. In bypass mode, natural gas flows through the reformer chamber unreacted. Energy efficiency was calculated as the ratio of reformer power consumption to total engine power output. Multiple plasma on/off cycles were conducted to confirm the observed effects. The reformer housing design was pressure-rated to 100 psig, exceeding anticipated operating conditions. Nitrogen purging was performed prior to plasma ignition to remove residual oxygen. All test operations complied with SwRI safety protocols for handling flammable gases and high-voltage equipment. SECTION 3 — Results and Discussion 3.1 Overview of Performance Evaluation The plasma fuel reformer was evaluated through a sequence of bench-scale, facility-scale, and engine-integration tests to verify plasma stability, methane conversion, and overall leak-reduction performance. Testing confirmed that the reformer design and pulsed power electrical system provided stable plasma operation across a wide range of gas-flow conditions, achieving measurable hydrogen and light-hydrocarbon formation consistent with design predictions. All experimental phases demonstrated that the system consumed less than one percent of the host engine’s power output while achieving meaningful methane reduction, satisfying DOE programmatic performance criteria. 3.2 Bench-Scale Performance Initial experiments were conducted to characterize plasma ignition, electrical behavior, and gas- phase chemistry under controlled bench-scale conditions.
